To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
In patients with left-sided breast cancer, an increase of the cardiac biomarker hscTn-T was found during adjuvant breast cancer RT.
The increase in hsc-TnT during RT is associated with higher cardiac radiation doses for whole heart and LV and that this increase may cause subclinical cardiac dysfunction.
the increase in hsc TnT level during RT was positively associated to cardiac radiation doses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the acute cardiac response to RT in breast cancer patients.
the acute subclinical changes of hscTnt levels during RT, and the association with cardiac radiation dose and echocardiography parameters.
the question whether the cardiac radiation doses should be reduced to minimize cardiac damage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hscTn T-release is associated with cardiac radiation doses, but the clinical implications remain to be elucidated.
the radiation dose to the heart should not exceed 5 Gy in any case, and the dose to the left ventricle should not exceed 3 Gy in any patient.
hscTn-T release during breast radiotherapy is associated with cardiac radiation doses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the radiation doses to the heart and LV should be minimized to reduce cardiac toxicity in breast cancer patients.
the radiation doses to the whole heart, left ventricle and left anterior descending artery are the most important predictors for an acute increase in hsc-TnT level.
cardiac morbidity and cardiac mortality can be reduced by avoiding high doses of radiation to the heart and LAD during RT.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of hscTNT as a marker of radiation induced cardiac injury is feasible.
cardiac radiation doses are an independent predictor of hscTnt increase.
the heart should be protected during left-sided breast cancer irradiation.
